newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Sweden's Nordbanken eyes buyback.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sweden's Nordbanken eyes buyback.

text.p: One of Sweden's big four banks, state-controlled Nordbanken, on Wednesday proposed a five billion crown ($741 million) share buyback scheme which analysts saw as paving the way for a merger or takeover.
Nordbanken said the buyback would reduce the number of its shares on the market by 15-18 percent and boost earnings per share, lifting its share price. The shares jumped on the news.

It would also lower the government's stake to 58 percent from 65.5 percent, furthering the state's intentions to divest its holding in the bank it bailed out in 1992 when it faced collapse after a loan-loss crisis.

"The bottom line is that they are doing it to raise the value of their shares so that they can get better terms in any potential merger or takeover situation," Kleinwort Benson banking analyst Keith Baird told Reuters.
Analysts were convinced that Nordbanken was heading towards a takeover or merger based on a share deal, not cash.
For months industry analysts have tipped Nordbanken as the bank most likely to succeed in a takeover of mortgage institute Stadshypotek.
Nordbanken has a strong, stable retail banking franchise but Stadshypotek's home loan business would help it compete with arch-rival Swedbank in this lucrative area.
"If they bid for Stadshypotek with shares this will reduce the state's holding in the bank further and then it would be able to sell the rest in one tranche," Matteus analyst Goran Kallebo said.

Nordbanken admitted the share buy back scheme was designed to give it more flexibility in Sweden's restructuring financial market where cash-rich banks are vying for position as the industry braces itself for a shake-out.

"The increased profit per share should be positive for the market share price which will improve our chance to take an active part in the continuing restructure of Sweden's financial sector," managing director Hans Dalborg said in a statement.
The bank said the scheme, open from September 23 to October 11, would buy back shares at a price three percent below the market price in a range of 130-155 crowns.
Bank chairman Jacob Palmstierna said the bank currently had 19.7 billion capital and would use remaining funds to expand.

"It is the board and the management's view that the remaining capital is easily enough for possible future expansion, especially considering the bank's continuing profitability," Palmstierna said in a statement.
The news was received positively by the market with the bank's shares jumping 14.5 crowns to 150 crowns within five minutes of trading. It closed at 149 crowns.
"We are very positive about this," said analyst Per Griberg from Carnegie. "The increase in the share price is justified."
The government also gave its backing to the proposal. Finance Minister Erik Askbrink said the buy back would further improve the health of the bank and was a step towards denationalisation.
"The government stands by its intention to sell off the entire state holding in Nordbanken," he said in a statement.
"The state will place its entire holding in the sale programme so that the programme can be successfully completed independently of the sign-up rate of other shareholders."
Nordbanken in August reported an 18 percent jump in first half profit, after credit losses, to 3.8 billion crowns.
